Shebna
sheb'nä
n. (the treasurer and scribe of Hezekiah's court, denounced by Isaiah for hewing himself a sepulchre on high and deposed from his stewardship)
From Hebrew Shebna or Shebnah, probably from a root meaning vigour or youthfulness. The Authorized Version calls him treasurer at Isaiah 22:15 and scribe at 2 Kings 18:18 — the same man in two stations, the second lower than the first.

Biblical Definition

Shebna is the court official of Hezekiah's reign whom the LORD singled out by name for judgment, and the only steward in Scripture whose deposition is prophesied in advance and then quietly recorded as accomplished. Isaiah is sent to him with a stinging errand: “Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house” (Isa 22:15). The charge is not embezzlement or treason but a monument. “What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here” (Isa 22:16) — a foreigner by every indication, with no father named and no inheritance in the land, cutting himself a rock-tomb among the graves of Judah's great men so that the nation would have to remember him. The sentence is stated plainly: “I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down” (Isa 22:19), and the office is handed to another: “I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah” (Isa 22:20). By the time Sennacherib's army stands at the conduit, the transfer has happened. Eliakim is “over the household” and Shebna is merely “the scribe” (2Ki 18:18). He is still useful, still trusted enough to be sent to Isaiah in sackcloth (2Ki 19:2), but he is no longer over the house. God demoted him and then kept him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Shebna; in sacred history he is Hezekiah's treasurer, deposed from the stewardship of the house and left as scribe.

expand to see more

SHEBNA, n. An officer of the court of Hezekiah king of Judah.

He was over the house, that is, steward or comptroller of the royal household.

Isaiah was sent to reprove him for hewing out a sepulchre for himself in the rock.

His station was given to Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and he was made scribe.

In that lower office he was sent with Eliakim to the prophet in the year of Sennacherib.

Key Scripture

Isa 22:15 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say,"

Isa 22:16 — "What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?"

Isa 22:19 — "And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down."

Isa 22:21 — "And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah."

Modern Corruption

The modern misuse is to read Shebna's fall as a lesson in personal branding gone wrong. Scripture reads it as the LORD's judgment on a steward who used a trust to build a name, and as the occasion for a promise that reaches past Eliakim to Christ.

expand to see more

Shebna is handled today, when he is handled at all, as a cautionary tale about ego in leadership — a management failure with a spiritual veneer. That reading empties the oracle. Isaiah does not tell Shebna he has damaged his effectiveness; he tells him the LORD will drive him from his station. The sin named is not poor self-awareness but the theft of a stewardship: a man set over another man's house who spent the house's resources carving his own memorial into it. That is the standing temptation of every officer of the church, and Scripture treats it as a matter for divine sentence, not for coaching.

The passage also carries a promise the pulpit must not surrender to management-speak. Of Eliakim the LORD says, “the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isa 22:22), and the risen Christ takes those very words for Himself: “he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth” (Rev 3:7). Even Eliakim, the better steward, is warned that the nail in the sure place will one day be cut down (Isa 22:25). Every human steward is temporary; only One holds the key by right. Shebna's tomb is the monument of a servant who forgot he was one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shebna (H7644), Shebna; sokén (H5532), treasurer, steward; bayith (H1004), house, household; qeber (H6913), grave, sepulchre; maddaph — see rather hadaph (H1920), to thrust or drive out.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shebna (H7644) — Shebna; the treasurer over Hezekiah's house.

Hebrew sokén (H5532) — treasurer, steward; the office Isaiah names in the summons.

Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house; ‘over the house’ is the technical title of the chief officer.

Hebrew qeber (H6913) — grave, sepulchre; the monument Shebna hewed for himself.

Hebrew hadaph (H1920) — to thrust away, drive out; the verb of his deposition.

Usage

"“Go, get thee unto this treasurer” — the LORD sends a prophet to one bureaucrat by name."

"“What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here?” — a man with no roots buying himself a monument."

"“And Shebna the scribe” — the demotion recorded without comment, four chapters later."
